narratives.Description: bug(session,hooks): claim, release and grant resolve the occupancy actor by three different rules, so the printed recovery is unreachable and a parent locks out its own children
narratives.Overview:
## Summary

The occupancy actor is resolved by three different rules on three surfaces of the same lease. The claim path resolves a host-published owner. The release path does not. The grant path prints a placeholder the party it addresses cannot compute. The result is that a session can claim a lease it cannot release, and a parent can lock out its own children in the same checkout, with every printed recovery unreachable from the state that printed it.

This is the residue measured after #3873 / PR #3948 (squash `41331dea`) landed the identity transport. It is filed separately rather than grown onto that scope, which is delivered.

Origin of the measurements: https://github.com/deftai/directive/issues/3873#issuecomment-5469266268

## Measured on 2026-08-30

### 1. Claim and release disagree on who the actor is

`resolveOccupancySessionId` falls through to `ambientHostSessionOwner`, so a claim on a Grok host binds the lease to `host:grok:v1:<base64url(GROK_SESSION_ID)>`.

`releaseOccupancy` (`packages/core/src/session/occupancy.ts:742-743`) resolves the caller as:

```ts
const caller =
  input.sessionId?.trim() || (input.env ?? process.env).DEFT_SESSION_ID?.trim() || "";
```

It never consults `ambientHostSessionOwner`. `packages/cli/src/occupancy-release.ts:56-59` passes `sessionId: undefined`. `git show --stat 41331dea` confirms PR #3948 never touched that file.

Measured against the built modules at HEAD: `releaseOccupancy(root, { env })` returns `action: denied`, `code: 1`, `caller: ""`, and the lease survives. Passing the id explicitly releases cleanly.

Consequence on the installed 0.108.0 runtime, reproduced live: `task session:start` claimed a lease under a minted id, the next tool-call write was denied naming that same id, and `task occupancy:release` minted another id and was refused as a stranger. The only recovery that worked was `task occupancy:release -- --session-id <the-id-the-deny-reported>`. The deny text says "The occupant may release (`occupancy:release` / `session:end`)", which is the one thing the occupant cannot do.

### 2. A parent locks out its own children

`GROK_SESSION_ID` is per-agent-session and is **not** inherited by subagents. Two Grok sessions on the same workspace seven seconds apart derived different canonical owners, and the second session's write against the first session's live lease was denied.

This differs from Codex, where the host identity source is documented as shared between parent and subagents (`packages/core/src/hooks/classify/host-session-identity.ts`). So on Grok the lease is per-agent, while the worktree it guards is per-cohort.

The printed remediation is `occupancy:grant --child-session-id=<your-session-id>`, run by the occupant. The child cannot supply its own canonical string without base64url-encoding the environment variable itself, and the occupant does not have it.

### 3. An out-of-tree write is gated by the payload root's lease

A write to an OS temp path was denied by the primary checkout's lease. An out-of-tree target has no worktree of its own, so `effectiveRoot` falls back to the payload root. The lease is therefore not confined to the checkout it describes: it serialises writes anywhere the agent touches. With 100+ worktrees under `.deft-scratch/worktrees/`, that coupling widens as cohort size grows.

## Why this is not a #3873 regression

#3873's bound acceptance covers the claim-and-present loop, and that loop works: claiming under the host owner and presenting the same owner yields an occupancy admission, with an unidentified actor still denied. None of its six clauses covers the release path, the parent/child case, or out-of-tree gating. This issue is the part that was never in scope, surfaced by operating the fixed design.

## Not asserted -- for the critic and builder to establish

1. Whether release should accept the recorded occupant id from the lease when the caller can present no identity, or whether that weakens the fail-closed posture the #3611 decision record protects.
2. Whether the parent/child case is an identity problem (children should derive a related owner) or a membership problem (`occupancy:grant` should be automatic within a nuclear-family cohort, #3155).
3. Whether an out-of-tree write target should be gated by the payload root at all, or whether `effectiveRoot` should decline to fall back.
4. Whether the three surfaces should share one actor-resolution function, and what that does to the locked unsupported-host tests.
5. Whether any of this is safe to change before the identity transport ships in a release; the fix is merged but unreleased, so operators are currently on the pre-fix runtime.

## Design-critique

`mechanism-shaped: true`

Refs #3873, #3611, #3755, #3433, #3794, #3155, #3156.

New datum on frequency: the lockout re-fired after `git checkout -b` inside the worktree, because the ritual saw HEAD change discontinuously, prompted `session:ready`, re-claimed, and re-armed the same deny. So the cost is once per branch switch inside a single worker, not once per session.

At 2026-08-31T08:15Z a write to a path under `%TEMP%` was denied by the primary checkout's lease, naming the then-occupant. The path was not the discriminator; the tool surface was, which is #3987 rather than this issue -- recorded here only so the section 3 measurement is not read as path-scoped.

The lease that denied the parent session at 08:15Z was held by `host:claude:v1:MDFhMDU1ZTItYjUwMy03YjcyLWEwNTQtYjlkZmY1YmM1ZTMy` (`claimed_at` 03:37:24Z) and carried one grant:

  "child_session_id": "host:grok:v1:MDFhMDU1ZTItYjUwMy03YjcyLWEwNTQtYjlkZmY1YmM1ZTMy",

Both strings carry the same payload, which decodes to `01a055e2-b503-7b72-a054-b9dff5bc5e32` -- the Claude session's own raw id, re-prefixed as a Grok owner. No Grok session would ever present that string; the Grok session actually running presented `01a055fb-...` and was denied. So a grant can be recorded for a child id that cannot exist, and it reads as membership while admitting nobody. That is the grant-path half of section 1 observed from the granted side.

Ceiling honored: #3954 comment 5480092795 inclusive. I filtered the REST response by id before reading it and did not inspect later comments. Measured checkout: fb9ece05 on master.

## Verdict

The portfolio claim survives only with amendments. Keep both issues: #3954 is the actor-resolution and membership-reachability prerequisite; #3999 is a distinct lifecycle-termination problem. They compose if #3954 lands first and #3999 releases only an exact child lease at an exact worktree after independently observed completion. They should not be merged, and neither dominates the other. The identity-versus-membership question is settleable once as a layering rule, not as one shared identity: resolve each actor canonically, preserve per-agent identity, and represent parent/child authority as explicit, bounded membership.

I re-ran seven focused Vitest files (137 tests, all passed), including occupancy, Grok identity, host-identity lifetime, effective-root, release CLI, and cohort close-out tests. I also probed `packages/core/dist/session/occupancy.js`: with only `GROK_SESSION_ID`, claim used `host:grok:v1:Y3JpdGljLXByb2Jl`; bare release returned denied with caller `""`; bare grant returned configuration denial with owner `""`; explicit release under that canonical owner succeeded. The built artifact was present. I did not treat parent comment 5479986245 as confirmation; the claims below come from source, the probe, and tests.

## blocks-the-design - #3999 - dispatcher-side release has no defined completion boundary

Evidence: `swarm:launch` persists a parent `occupancy_session_id` but explicitly stops before host spawn (`packages/core/src/swarm/launch.ts:1102-1116, 1253-1277`). The PreToolUse spawn path is pre-dispatch only and deliberately skips occupancy (`packages/core/src/hooks/dispatcher.ts:1192-1195, 1256-1266`). `agent:monitor` can read a terminal heartbeat, but that heartbeat is worker-authored (`packages/core/src/orchestration/subagent-monitor.ts:139-190`); `complete-cohort` releases the cohort owner's lease from its launch record, not an ad-hoc child's lease (`packages/core/src/swarm/complete-cohort.ts:620-655`).

Failure mode: a design that merely says the parent releases on child completion has no repository event on which to fire. Making the worker write a terminal record and making the parent remember to consume it reproduces the process-only gap #3999 reports. A killed worker also emits no terminal heartbeat.

Disposition consequence: retain #3999, but it is not mechanism-shaped enough to build until it names a host-neutral completion adapter or deterministic parent close-out primitive, plus the durable tuple it consumes: child canonical actor, exact worktree root, dispatch id, and terminal evidence. Its acceptance test must drive that boundary, not mock a direct `releaseOccupancy` call and call it worker lifecycle.

## blocks-the-design - the set - recorded-occupant release is not a safe unifier

Evidence: #3755 deliberately makes occupancy a cooperative bearer-id boundary and keeps release owner-only (`packages/core/src/session/occupancy.ts:5-20, 730-806`). #3611 also treats host ids as classification, not authentication (`packages/core/src/session/host-session-owner.ts:1-10`). Current release rechecks the owner under the lock before unlinking; the focused tests include non-owner denial and changed-owner fencing.

Failure mode: allowing an unidentified caller or a generic parent to read `occupancy.json` and release its recorded owner turns possession of the file path into live-lease deletion authority. A delayed child-completion event could also erase a successor's lease unless cleanup compares the registered child id with the current lease owner under the lock. In a swarm, a wrong worktree or stale sibling notification makes that cross-session race concrete.

Disposition consequence: #3954 open question 1 must resolve against anonymous recorded-owner release. #3999 may use delegated cleanup only when a dispatch record proves the exact child/root pair and the atomic release still finds that child as current owner. Otherwise it must no-op or fail closed. This is the injection/swarm constraint: bounded nuclear-family topology is not ambient administrative authority.

## sharpens-framing - #3954 - identity and membership are separate layers

Evidence: the dist probe reproduced the real divergence: `resolveOccupancySessionId` includes `ambientHostSessionOwner`, while release and grant resolve only explicit `sessionId` or `DEFT_SESSION_ID` (`packages/core/src/session/occupancy.ts:437-454, 730-744, 847-865`). But #3873 already makes the denied writer's actual canonical id available in remediation, and the Grok test grants that exact id successfully (`packages/core/src/hooks/dispatcher-grok-identity.test.ts:237-263`). Comment 5479986245's impossible grant therefore does not prove the grant mechanism generated that child id; no production path for constructing that malformed cross-provider value was established.

Failure mode: making parent and child derive one family owner would erase per-agent attribution and contradict #3755's explicit grant record. Conversely, leaving grant's owner resolver divergent means the parent may know the correct child id and still be unable to run the bare grant on Grok. Automatic membership inferred anywhere from a matching string would duplicate the existing grant mechanism and weaken its role, expiry, and worktree record.

Disposition consequence: narrow #3954 to one shared actor-resolution policy for owner-side operations (release, grant/revoke, heartbeat, and claim where mint fallback remains intentional), with operation-specific no-identity behavior. Keep child identity distinct. If automatic membership is desired, issue the existing bounded grant only at a dispatcher edge that has independently established the exact child id and worktree; do not add lineage inference inside occupancy.

## sharpens-framing - #3999 - the claimed worktree is required evidence

Evidence: #3999 explicitly did not capture `worktree_path`. Existing #3794 behavior resolves direct writes to the linked target worktree: the focused effective-root tests passed cases where a primary lease does not block a linked-worktree write and where the linked worktree's own lease does (`packages/core/src/hooks/dispatcher-effective-root.test.ts:202-282`). Session commands, however, act on their resolved project root. These facts do not establish which root the reported worker actually claimed.

Failure mode: cleanup keyed only by child id can release the wrong checkout, while an acceptance claim that the parent was locked out may be false if the residue lived in a disposable child worktree. Deleting a worktree could also remove its local `.deft/occupancy.json`, making a later root-level sweep target a different lease.

Disposition consequence: keep the stranded-lease recurrence as #3999's premise, but make exact-root capture part of dispatch and of the dispatch-claim-exit test. Treat the parent-self-lockout sentence as conditional until that test reproduces a child claiming the parent's root. This does not remove the lifecycle defect; it prevents choosing a cleanup mechanism from an unmeasured location.

## sharpens-framing - the set - land #3954 before #3999, but do not claim a hard runtime dependency

Evidence: explicit child-id release succeeds today, so a carefully implemented dispatcher cleanup is technically possible before shared actor resolution. Bare worker-side release does not succeed on Grok, as the dist probe showed. #3987 improves observation of shell writes, but Grok is intentionally absent from the updated-input wire (`packages/core/src/hooks/dispatcher.ts:1921-1932`), so it does not transport the owner into Grok lifecycle commands. It therefore composes with this set but does not settle its actor rule.

Failure mode if inverted: #3999 can grow a one-off explicit-id cleanup path while operator release, grant, and heartbeat remain governed by a different actor rule. A later worker-side fallback then fails on the same host, and tests accidentally bless two identity policies. The reverse order leaves lifecycle residue temporarily, but it establishes the primitive every close-out path should consume.

Disposition consequence: land #3954 first as the shared owner-resolution contract and tests, then #3999 as exact dispatch-lifecycle cleanup. Keep separate issues and make #3999 depend on the actor contract. Do not state that inversion is unreachable; state that it creates avoidable semantic duplication.

## footnote - #3999 - existing expiry and cohort cleanup do not dominate the issue

The inventory confirms #3599 heartbeat/age-cap and the 20-minute stale TTL bound residue but do not observe process exit. #3604 supplies ordinary release and `session:end`; #3604's cohort arm is exercised by `complete-cohort`, and the focused sweep tests passed. None is an ad-hoc host-child completion callback. #3999 therefore remains a real gap after its completion boundary and root evidence are specified.

## Road not taken and flip conditions

The strongest merge case is that one occupancy-lifecycle story could share fixtures and change actor resolution plus child cleanup atomically. I reject it because the first half is a pure actor-policy correction, while the second currently lacks an executable completion event and root provenance; merging would let uncertainty in #3999 delay the independently reproducible #3954 fix.

I also reject automatic family identity. Its best case is zero grant ceremony and immediate same-checkout cooperation, but it trades away attribution and contradicts the existing explicit, expiring membership model. I would flip to one merged issue if a host-neutral post-completion callback already exists and supplies a verified child canonical id plus exact worktree, allowing one small compare-and-release primitive to close both. I would close #3999 as dominated if a reconstructed dispatch-claim-exit run proves every affected lease is confined to a worktree that host cleanup always deletes, with no surviving lease or parent lockout. I would reverse the landing order only if #3999 chooses an explicit registered-child cleanup path whose tests never invoke ambient actor resolution and #3954 is independently delayed.

**Evidence.** At `fb9ece05`, `resolveOccupancySessionId` falls through to `ambientHostSessionOwner` (`occupancy.ts` claim path). `releaseOccupancy` caller resolution is only `input.sessionId || env.DEFT_SESSION_ID` (lines 742-743); `packages/cli/src/occupancy-release.ts` passes through optional `--session-id` and otherwise leaves ambient host unused. ### blocks-the-design — #3999: "parent minted the child session id" premise on Grok

**Evidence.** `GROK_SESSION_ID` is a `host-env` source; Codex is payload `session_id` shared parent/subagent (`host-session-identity.ts`). Probe: two different raw Grok ids yield two different `host:grok:v1:…` owners. Swarm close-out already refuses to invent identity from `occupancy.json` (`releaseSwarmOccupancy` comment: close-out identity from launch manifest or `DEFT_SESSION_ID` — never the lease file). Ad-hoc babysit dispatch (#3999 measured case) has no `persistLaunchOccupancyRecord`.

**Failure mode.** Implementing preferred shape 1 as "parent releases what it minted at spawn" releases nothing useful, or releases the wrong tree's lease if the parent substitutes its own id. Self-lockout within TTL remains.

**Disposition.** Keep #3999, but rewrite candidate 1's prerequisite: durable observation/record of the child's **presented host owner** (claim time / ritual / launch-equivalent slot), then parent release with that explicit id. Do not treat spawn tool args as occupancy identity on Grok.

**Evidence.** Occupancy header (#3755) is explicit: cooperative bearer-id boundary, **not** lineage; membership is `grantOccupancyMembership`, write-only; release/steal/heartbeat/close-out stay owner-only. #3954 Q2 asks whether Grok parent/child should share identity or get automatic membership. #3999's stranded lease is an **owner** lease left after exit; a live grant does not authorize release, and auto-granting a dead child's id does not clear the owner record.

Grants accumulate theater membership while owner leases still strand until TTL (#3604 recurrence class returns). Or the set flips Grok to shared identity (Codex-like) and calls #3999 done, while ad-hoc workers still never run close-out.

**Disposition.** Answer #3954 Q2 on its own (and against #3755's deliberate non-lineage). Answer #3999 as lifecycle close-out for owner leases on dispatch shapes that lack `complete-cohort`. Do not merge those decisions into one chip.

### sharpens-framing — #3954: grant path already admits unpresentable cross-prefix children

**Evidence.** Re-derived the 5479986245 grant shape at `fb9ece05`: owner `host:claude:v1:<b64(raw)>` granting `host:grok:v1:<b64(same raw)>` is accepted (`action:granted`); a real different Grok child is denied; presenting the bogus grok-prefixed string is admitted as `member`.
